subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage: Ojas's eyes had been wet since assembly, when Class 5 laughed at his wrong answer. He held it in until the corridor, then stopped at the water fountain and pretended to drink, breathing in slowly, out slowly. Trisha, the school counsellor, was passing. "Ojas?" He shook his head. "I want to be by myself." "That's okay. I'm in the room at the end of the hall if you want to talk." He nodded. After lunch he knocked. "Miss, I felt stupid. Everyone laughed." Trisha listened. "That sounds really hard," she said. Ojas wiped his face with his sleeve and breathed out, a little lighter.

qa.q: Where did Ojas stop to hide his tears?
qa.a: He stopped at the water fountain.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling in the corridor, and why did he later knock on Trisha's door?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed after being laughed at. He knocked later because being alone and breathing helped, and he then felt ready to tell a trusted adult.

qa.q: What could Ojas do if he keeps feeling low for a long time?
qa.a: He can keep talking with Trisha or another trusted adult, and they can help him work out what more support he needs.

qa.q: How does Trisha's response make it easier for Ojas?
qa.a: She does not push him and says where she is, so he can choose when to talk. Her calm listening helps him feel safe.

grounding: A child learns to breathe slowly, cry in private and tell a trusted adult about hurt.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage: Aditi noticed her classmate Zainab drawing less. For three weeks the girl who filled every margin with cats had left her page blank. She'd stopped joining games at recess, too. Today when the teacher praised her science project, Zainab said thank you very quietly and looked away. In the bathroom later, Aditi heard soft crying and left quickly. Back at her desk Zainab's eyes were red. Aditi wasn't sure whether to say anything. After school she told her mother, who said to tell the teacher what she had seen. Next day Aditi did, and the teacher said she was glad to know.

qa.q: For how many weeks had Zainab left her page blank?
qa.a: She had left it blank for three weeks.

qa.q: What might Zainab's quiet thank you and red eyes suggest she was feeling, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: They suggest she was sad and maybe struggling for some time, since she had also stopped drawing and joining games. It could also be a passing bad patch, which is why an adult should be told.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to support Zainab?
qa.a: She could invite Zainab to sit with her at recess, be kind without pushing, and keep telling a teacher or trusted adult, as she did.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when the teacher learns and gently checks in?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that someone noticed, or embarrassed at first. Having an adult who cares can lighten the load.

grounding: A child cries in private, and a long low mood with lost interest deserves adult attention, as an observer tells a teacher.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: At school, Rajni wasn't picked for the relay team. She walked to the bathroom, locked the door, and cried quietly into her sleeve. Then she breathed slowly, washed her face and went back to class.
Two weeks later: Rajni hadn't touched her sketchbook since that day, though she used to draw every evening. She ate little and went to bed early. Her aunt Himani noticed the sketchbook gathering dust on the shelf.
That evening: Himani sat beside her. "You haven't drawn for two weeks. You seem low. What's going on?"
Rajni burst into tears and told her about the relay and feeling left out since. Himani listened, hugged her, and said, "Thank you for telling me." That night she phoned Rajni's mother, and they agreed to talk to the class teacher together the next morning.

qa.q: What had Rajni not touched for two weeks?
qa.a: Her sketchbook.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling after not being picked for the relay?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad, crying privately in the bathroom and then staying low and uninterested for weeks.

qa.q: What did Himani do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed the long low mood and lost interest, gently asked about it the same day, listened, and involved Rajni's mother and teacher.

qa.q: How might Himani feel after hearing Rajni's story?
qa.a: Himani likely felt concerned and relieved that Rajni finally shared her feelings, and wanted to help quickly.

grounding: Across weeks, a child regulates sadness privately, but a long low mood with lost interest leads a trusted adult to step in.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage:
"Joseph, you think grown-ups never cry? When I was a girl in Kochi, I, Maria, had a dog called Bruno. One day he got sick and died. I didn't want anyone to see me cry, so I climbed up the jackfruit tree and cried there where no one could see.
I did that every afternoon for a week. I told no one. I stopped playing with my cousins, stopped reading. My Appachan noticed and waited under the tree one day. He said, 'Maria, you've been sad for a long time. Come down and talk to me.'
I did, and I cried in his arms. It felt so much better to share it. So if you're ever sad for a long time, you tell me, okay?"

qa.q: Where did Maria go to cry as a girl?
qa.a: Up the jackfruit tree.

qa.q: What was young Maria feeling that week after Bruno died?
qa.a: She felt deep sadness and was lonely, hiding her tears and losing interest in playing and reading.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Maria?
qa.a: Her Appachan chose to notice her long sadness and waited to talk with her, encouraging her to share.

qa.q: How might Appachan have felt waiting under the tree?
qa.a: He probably felt worried and gentle, wanting to help Maria stop hiding her sadness.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding sadness after a pet's death and how a trusted adult helped when the low mood lasted.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage:
Ramesh wasn't picked for the school cricket team, and he had a maths exam tomorrow. At home, the TV was loud, his little cousins were running around, and there was nowhere quiet.
He went up to the terrace. His eyes stung, and he let a few tears come. Then he breathed in slowly, counting to four, and out to six, like Dilnaz Aunty had taught him.
He felt a little calmer, but still sad.
He went next door. Dilnaz Aunty, who helped him with maths, opened the door. "Ramesh? What's wrong?"
"I didn't make the team," he said, voice shaky.
She let him sit and listened, then said, "That's hard. Let's do ten minutes of maths, then we can talk more."

qa.q: Where did Ramesh go to cry?
qa.a: Up to the terrace.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when his eyes stung?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed about not being picked for the team, and stressed about the exam.

qa.q: What small steps helped Ramesh manage his sadness?
qa.a: He cried privately, breathed slowly, and then chose to tell a trusted adult, Dilnaz Aunty.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz Aunty feel when Ramesh came to her?
qa.a: She probably felt caring and glad he trusted her enough to share his hurt.

grounding: Under exam pressure, a child regulates sadness by crying privately, breathing slowly, and telling a trusted adult.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage: When the list went up outside the sports room and his name wasn't on it, Jatin walked calmly to the boys' toilets, locked a cubicle and cried into his sleeve for a few minutes. Then he breathed slowly, splashed his face and went back to class. At home in Nagpur, Nikita Bua, who was staying with the family, noticed his cricket bat leaning in the corner again, the way it had been for two weeks. "You haven't played in the lane since the trials," she said gently. Jatin shrugged, and then the words came out: the list, the sleeve, how nothing felt fun. Bua listened and said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's tell your mum tonight too." After dinner, the three of them sat on the balcony and talked.

qa.q: Where did Jatin cry after seeing the list?
qa.a: In a locked cubicle in the boys' toilets.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he saw the list?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed enough to cry, though he chose to do it privately and then calm himself.

qa.q: Which of Jatin's ways of handling sadness helped, and what was missing at first?
qa.a: Crying privately and breathing slowly got him through class; what was missing was telling a trusted adult, which happened when Bua asked.

qa.q: How does Nikita Bua see the bat left in the corner?
qa.a: She reads it as a sign that Jatin's low mood has lasted, since he hasn't played for two weeks, so she gently opens a conversation.

grounding: It illustrates a child crying privately and breathing slowly, and an adult noticing lasting low mood and lost interest and bringing in a parent.
